problem:
$$
\overset{A}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}| & | & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} & {a}_{3} \\ | & | & |\end{aligned}]}}=\overset{Q}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}| & | & | \\ {q}_{1} & {q}_{2} & {q}_{3} \\ | & | & |\end{aligned}]}}\overset{R}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}{r}_{11} & {r}_{12} & {r}_{13} \\ 0 & {r}_{22} & {r}_{23} \\ 0 & 0 & {r}_{33}\end{aligned}]}}
$$

Consider the QR factorization of the matrix $A$ shown above. You're given that the system of equations given below connects the columns of $Q$ and the columns of $A.$  

$$
{\begin{aligned}{q}_{1}=\frac{1}{4}{a}_{1} \\ {q}_{2}=\frac{1}{2}{a}_{2}+{q}_{1} \\ {q}_{3}=\frac{1}{3}{a}_{3}+2{q}_{1}-{q}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

What is the value of ${r}_{13}+{r}_{22}+{r}_{23}?$

examples.knowledge_point: Finding a QR Factorization of a Matrix Given an Orthogonal Basis in Terms of the Columns of a Matrix
examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14093486/assets/3fb28ec29732f0bdc394079d31a08ae597ca1081aed8bb3df0e1219b5fa11a95.png)

Consider the QR factorization of the matrix $A$ shown above, where $\big\{ \mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_2,\mathbf{v}_3 \big\}$ is an orthogonal set of vectors. You're given that $\Vert\mathbf{v}_1\Vert =2,$ $\Vert\mathbf{v}_2\Vert =3,$ $\Vert\mathbf{v}_3\Vert =4,$ and that the system of equations below describes the relationship between the columns of $Q$ and the columns of $A.$

$$
{\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}={a}_{1} \\ {v}_{2}={a}_{2}-{v}_{1} \\ {v}_{3}={a}_{3}-3{v}_{1}+2{v}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

What is the value of $r_{13}+r_{23}+r_{33}?$
examples.worked_solution:
First, we normalize the vectors $\mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_2,\mathbf{v}_3 \mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}_{1} & =\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{{v}_{1}}{2}\,⟹\,{v}_{1}=2{q}_{1} \\ {q}_{2} & =\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{{v}_{2}}{3}\,⟹\,{v}_{2}=3{q}_{2} \\ {q}_{3} & =\frac{{v}_{3}}{‖{v}_{3}‖}=\frac{{v}_{3}}{4}\,⟹\,{v}_{3}=4{q}_{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the set $\big\{ \mathbf{q}_1,\mathbf{q}_2,\mathbf{q}_3 \big\}$ will be both orthogonal and normalized.

Next, let's rewrite the vectors $\mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2, \mathbf{a}_3$ as a linear combination of the vectors $\mathbf{q}_1, \mathbf{q}_2, \mathbf{q}_3 \mathbin{:}$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14093486/assets/2b733751d472729343a3c74af43339f89e9b6142593425d7bf45c912a8f27b4f.png)

The final system can be written in matrix form as follows:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14093486/assets/d396c0e50ecbcf618674f01cc24e1c70075be96343138cd8a6d04548b19c5049.png)

Therefore, 

$$
r_{13}+r_{23}+r_{33} = 6+(-6)+4 = 4.
$$

feedback.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}],\,Q=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{3}{\sqrt{22}} \\ 0 & \frac{2}{\sqrt{22}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{3}{\sqrt{22}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices $A$ and $Q$ shown above. Find the matrix $R$ such that $A=QR$ is a QR factorization of $A.$
feedback.worked_solution:
Since $Q$ has orthonormal columns, pre-multiplying both sides of $A=QR$ by ${Q}^{T},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}^{T}\cdot A & ={Q}^{T}\cdot QR \\ {Q}^{T}A & =({Q}^{T}Q)R \\ {Q}^{T}A & ={I}_{2}R \\ R & ={Q}^{T}A\end{aligned}
$$

Note that ${Q}^{T}Q={I}_{2}$ since the columns of $Q$ are orthonormal.

Now, we calculate the matrix $R:$

$$
\begin{aligned}R & ={Q}^{T}A \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{22}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{22}} & -\frac{3}{\sqrt{22}}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{2} & \frac{3}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 & \frac{\sqrt{22}}{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$
